title: Layers and a small network
objectives: Build a layer and a multilayer perceptron from neurons, and count its parameters.

screens.title: One neuron draws one line
screens.prose: The course data has four points: $(1, 1)$ and $(-1, -1)$ with target 1, $(1, -1)$ and $(-1, 1)$ with target $-1$. The target is the sign of $x_1x_2$, an XOR. One tanh neuron changes sign along one straight line, $w_1x_1 + w_2x_2 + b = 0$.
screens.question: Can one neuron put both +1 points on one side of its line and both $-1$ points on the other?

options.text: No: the +1 points sit on one diagonal and the $-1$ points on the other, and no line splits them
Yes: the vertical line $x_1 = 0$ splits the four points into two pairs
options.why: That line puts $(1, 1)$ with $(1, -1)$, which have opposite targets.

options.text: Yes, as long as the weights are made large enough
options.why: Large weights make the line sharper, not bent. It is still one line.

options.text: Yes, by moving the bias far enough to one side
options.why: Moving the bias shifts the line until all four points are on one side.

hints.text: Try a few lines on the picture.
Any line that separates $(1, 1)$ from $(1, -1)$ also leaves $(-1, -1)$ or $(-1, 1)$ on the wrong side.
No single line works, so the network needs a hidden layer.

feedback.correct: No line works. A hidden layer of neurons gives several lines, which the output neuron combines.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Try to draw the line.

explain.text: The +1 points lie on one diagonal and the $-1$ points on the other, so every line leaves a wrong point on some side. A hidden layer lets the network combine several lines.

screens.title: A 2-3-1 network
screens.prose: The course network has 2 inputs, a hidden **layer** of 3 tanh neurons and 1 output neuron: a 2-3-1 **multilayer perceptron**. Each edge is a weight (width by size, blue positive, red negative); each neuron's bias is under it. Step the forward pass for the point $(1, 1)$.
screens.question: What does the network output at $(1, 1)$? Give 4 decimal places.

hints.text: The output neuron takes the three hidden values.

feedback.correct: $-0.3266$, far from the target 1: the untrained network is wrong here.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Read the output neuron in the last frame.

byKey.hidden: That is $h_1$. The output is the last neuron.
byKey.sign: The output is negative here, on the wrong side of the target 1.

explain.text: Each hidden neuron squashes its own weighted sum: $h = (-0.8079, 0.2662, -0.1954)$. The output neuron does the same with $h$ and gives $-0.3266$; the target at $(1, 1)$ is 1.

screens.title: Counting parameters
screens.prose: In code a `Neuron(nin)` holds `nin` weights and one bias; a `Layer(nin, nout)` holds `nout` neurons; an `MLP(nin, [3, 1])` chains layers of sizes 3 and 1. Every weight and bias is a **parameter** that training will move.
screens.question: How many parameters does the 2-3-1 network have?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Count every weight and every bias.

byKey.no-bias: You counted the 9 weights. Each of the 4 neurons also has a bias.
byKey.neurons: That counts the neurons. Each has several parameters.

explain.text: Each hidden neuron has 2 weights and a bias (9 in all), and the output neuron has 3 weights and a bias (4). That makes 13 parameters.

screens.title: Bigger networks
screens.prose: A layer from $m$ inputs to $k$ neurons has $mk$ weights and $k$ biases, $(m + 1)k$ parameters. A network adds its layers.
screens.question: Count the parameters of each network.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Add $(m + 1)k$ over the layers.

screens.title: Where the numbers come from
screens.prose: The parameters come from `random.Random(42).uniform(-1, 1)`, drawn in a fixed order: layer by layer, neuron by neuron, each neuron's weights then its bias. So the first three draws are $h_1$'s two weights and bias.
screens.question: Give the first three parameters, to 3 decimal places.

hints.text: Read $h_1$'s two edges and the bias under it.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Weights, then bias, one neuron at a time.

byKey.next-weight: You moved to $h_2$ too early. Each neuron takes its bias before the next neuron starts.

explain.text: Draws 1 to 3 fill $h_1$: weights 0.279 and $-0.950$, bias $-0.450$. Draws 4 to 6 fill $h_2$, and so on to the output's bias, draw 13. The same seed and order give the same network every time.

screens.title: Weights are not all
screens.prose: Sam sizes a 3-4-4-1 network by counting the edges in its drawing: $3 \times 4 + 4 \times 4 + 4 \times 1 = 32$. He writes 32 in his report.
screens.question: How many parameters does it really have?

hints.text: What does a drawing of edges leave out?
Every neuron also has a bias.

feedback.correct: $32 + 9 = 41$: the drawing shows weights, not biases.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Add a bias for every neuron.

byKey.no-bias: That is Sam's count: edges only. Each of the 9 neurons adds a bias.

explain.text: The edges are the 32 weights. The 4, 4 and 1 neurons add 9 biases, so the network has 41 parameters.

screens.title: No hidden layer
screens.prose: An edge case: drop the hidden layer and train one neuron, `MLP(2, [1])`, on the course data. Its loss, the sum of squared errors, starts at 6.6146 and stops falling.
screens.question: What loss does it settle at?

hints.text: With no line that fits, the best it can do is output 0 everywhere.

feedback.correct: It settles at 4: it outputs about 0 everywhere, missing every target by 1.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Read where the curve flattens.

byKey.zero: One neuron cannot fit an XOR; only the hidden layer lets the loss fall towards 0.

explain.text: No line splits the XOR, so the neuron's best move is to output 0 at all four points. Each misses by 1, so the loss settles at 4.

screens.title: Neuron, Layer and MLP
screens.prose: Write the three classes; the `Value` class with `tanh()` is loaded. `Neuron(nin, rng)` draws its weights then its bias from `rng.uniform(-1, 1)`. `Layer(nin, nout, rng)` makes `nout` neurons. `MLP(nin, nouts, seed=42)` makes one `random.Random(seed)` and builds the layers in order. Calling a neuron returns `tanh` of $\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x} + b$; a layer returns a list; an MLP returns the last layer's list, or its one Value.
screens.question: Write `Neuron`, `Layer` and `MLP`, each with `parameters()`.

widget.how: Submit runs 8 hidden tests: three parameter counts, the first five parameters for seed 42, two outputs at the initial parameters, a two-output network and the parameter types. Values are accepted when `math.isclose(actual, expected, rel_tol=1e-9)`.

mutants.symptom: draws the bias before the weights, so seed 42 gives the wrong parameters
a fresh generator per layer repeats the same draws
a one-output network returns a list instead of a `Value`

hints.text: A neuron's call: `sum((wi * xi for wi, xi in zip(self.w, x)), self.b).tanh()`.
`MLP` builds `Layer(sizes[i], sizes[i + 1], rng)` for each consecutive pair of `[nin] + nouts`, all sharing one `rng`.

feedback.correct: The classes build the course network: 13 parameters starting 0.278854, $-0.949978$, $-0.449941$, and an output of $-0.3266$ at $(1, 1)$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-4: Test 4 reads the first five parameters for seed 42: $h_1$'s weights and bias, then $h_2$'s two weights. Draw weights before the bias, and share one `rng`.
byKey.test-5: Test 5 is the output at $(1, 1)$: $-0.3266$. Apply `tanh` in every neuron, the output neuron included.

explain.text: One `rng` passed down the layers keeps the draws in the stated order, so seed 42 gives the same 13 numbers every time. Each class only lists its parts' parameters, and the MLP chains the layers' calls.

screens.title: A fund's small network
screens.prose: A fund fits a 5-8-8-1 network to five daily features to predict a nonlinear signal. It has one year of data: 250 trading days.
screens.question: How many parameters does the network have?

feedback.correct: 129 parameters from 250 days: about one parameter for every two observations, which is easy to overfit.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Count weights and biases per layer.

explain.text: $48 + 72 + 9 = 129$ parameters against 250 data points. With that ratio the network can fit noise; later courses (First language models, level 3, and Training Networks) measure it on held-out data.

ideas: One neuron splits the plane with one line, so it cannot fit an XOR; a hidden layer can.
A layer from $m$ inputs to $k$ neurons has $(m + 1)k$ parameters: 13 for 2-3-1, 41 for 3-4-4-1, 337 for 2-16-16-1.
Seeded draws in a fixed order (layer, neuron, weights then bias) give the same network every time.
summary.trap: Counting the edges of a drawing gives the weights only: 32 for 3-4-4-1, which has 41 parameters.

quiz.prose: A network is 4-2-1: four inputs, two hidden tanh neurons, one output.
quiz.question: How many parameters does it have?

explain.text: The hidden layer has $4 \times 2$ weights and 2 biases (10), the output 2 weights and a bias (3): 13 in all.

quiz.prose: An `MLP(2, [3, 1], seed=42)` draws its 13 parameters in the course order.
quiz.question: Which parameter is the 4th draw?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Weights then bias, one neuron at a time.

explain.text: $h_1$ takes draws 1 to 3 (two weights, then its bias). The 4th draw is $h_2$'s first weight.

quiz.question: What does calling it on a list of 5 inputs return?

options.text: A list of 3 Values, one per neuron

options.why: You used the input size. The layer has 3 neurons, one output each.

options.text: One Value, the sum of the neurons
options.why: A layer returns each neuron's output separately.
That is part of its parameters, not its output.

feedback.generic: Not quite. How many neurons does it have?

explain.text: `Layer(5, 3)` has 3 neurons, each reading all 5 inputs. Called, it returns their 3 outputs as a list.
